unit.title: Expressions, Equality, and Linear Equations
unit.act: Act II - Preserving truth while changing form
unit.role: Build the central equivalence engine of elementary algebra.
unit.governingQuestion: How can an equation change form without changing its solutions?
unit.storyArc: Students first test solutions, then use inverse operations and simplification to construct equivalent equations. The unit ends with strategy selection and one-variable modeling.
outcomes: Define a solution and solution set.
Construct equivalent linear equations using legal operations.
Solve equations containing parentheses, fractions, decimals, and variables on both sides.
unit.investigation: Reconstruct an original quantity after a sequence of fees, discounts, or changes.
unit.mastery: Mixed equations without method labels; students must show an equivalence-preserving chain and verify the result.

lessons.title: Solutions, solution sets, and checking
lessons.outcome: Determine whether candidate values make an equation true and distinguish a proposed answer from a verified solution.

opening.prompt: Test several possible access codes against a condition.
opening.purpose: Use a concrete situation to identify the quantities and decision that make solutions, solution sets, and checking necessary.

prerequisiteChecks: Name the known quantity, the unknown quantity, and any units in the opening situation.
Classify the central object as an expression, equation, inequality, relation, function, or numerical comparison.
State one earlier rule or representation you would use to check a result for solutions, solution sets, and checking.
exposition: Determine whether candidate values make an equation true and distinguish a proposed answer from a verified solution. Begin by naming the mathematical objects before manipulating them. In solutions, solution sets, and checking, notation compresses a relationship among quantities; it does not replace that relationship. Track what each symbol represents, preserve grouping and units, and mark any restriction or endpoint as soon as it appears. The first useful question is therefore not “Which memorized move do I use?” but “What must remain true from one line or representation to the next?”

Left/right value evaluator. Read the labels as mathematical evidence: identify what is fixed, what changes, and how the objects are related. Then connect that evidence to the symbolic work one justified step at a time. A correct transformation preserves the relevant value, truth set, rate, domain, or geometric feature. If a step changes one of those, it needs a stated condition and a check against the original problem.

Substitution check strip. Use the worked examples to compare symbolic, numerical, and visual forms. Each form should answer the same question, even when it emphasizes a different feature. Finish by interpreting the result in a complete sentence and checking it with substitution, estimation, units, graph position, or an inverse operation. That final check distinguishes a plausible-looking candidate from a supported conclusion.
